summary: Students aged 12-14 learn which combinations of a triangle's six measurements (three sides, three angles) force a UNIQUE triangle: SSS, SAS, ASA, plus the derived AAS, and RHS for right triangles. The core idea is DETERMINATION — which data over-determine, under-determine, or exactly fix a figure. Two hard points: (a) SSA (two sides and a NON-included angle) is ambiguous — the free 'swinging' side can meet the other arm of the angle in two places, giving zero, one or two triangles — yet students wrongly treat it like SAS because both are 'two sides and an angle'; (b) AAA fixes only SHAPE (similarity), not size, so equiangular triangles need not be congruent. Alongside sits the correspondence convention: △ABC ≅ △DEF means A↔D, B↔E, C↔F, so letter order encodes matching parts. The strongest learning comes from physically constructing triangles from given conditions and discovering for oneself when data over- or under-determine the figure.
misconceptions: Treating SSA as a valid criterion by conflating it with SAS — not checking whether the angle is included between the two sides
Believing AAA (equal angles) proves congruence, confusing congruence with similarity
Assuming any three given measurements determine a unique triangle
Mismatching corresponding parts — ignoring that the letter order in △ABC ≅ △DEF encodes the correspondence
Not realising AAS works (because the third angle is forced) while SSA does not

activities.title: Swing the non-included side: SSA's two triangles
steps: Set up a fixed 9 cm base line. At one end, mark a 40° angle, drawing the second arm of that angle as a long ray rising from the corner. Pin a 6 cm 'arm' at the FAR end of the base (so the 40° angle sits OPPOSITE the 6 cm side, not between the two sides).
BEFORE moving anything, predict in writing: how many triangles can you complete, and WHY?

Swing the 6 cm arm (physically, or draw a compass arc of radius 6 cm centred at the far end of the base) and mark every point where the arc crosses the OTHER arm of the 40° angle (the ray rising from the angled corner) — each crossing is a possible third vertex.
Count the crossing points and draw each complete triangle you find.

Reconfigure with the40-degree angle between the6cm and9cm sides. Fix both sides on the two rays and join their free endpoints; compare this lockedSAS construction with the freeSSA arc. Rotated or reflected copies are still congruent, not different-sized solutions.
State in your own words why moving the angle from 'opposite' to 'between' changes the number of triangles.
activities.insight: Two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) do NOT determine a unique triangle — the free side can swing to meet the other arm of the angle in up to two places. When the angle is INCLUDED between the two sides (SAS), the triangle is locked. 'Included' is the word that matters.

activities.title: Construct from conditions: when do data fix a triangle?
steps: Using ruler, protractor and compass (or a dynamic geometry tool), attempt to construct a triangle from each data set: SSS (three given sides), SAS (two sides with the angle between them), ASA (two angles with the side between them), SSA (two sides with an angle opposite one), and AAA (three given angles).
For each, record whether you got exactly one triangle, more than one, or none.
For AAA, construct a second triangle with the same three angles but longer sides; compare it to the first.
Fill in a one/none/many outcome table listing each data set and its result.
Explain for AAS why giving two angles and one side forces a unique triangle even though you were not told the third angle directly.
activities.insight: CompatibleSSS,SAS,ASA,AAS orRHS data determine a triangle up to congruence. Invalid measurements may determine none;SSA can allow zero,one or two, and validAAA data allow different sizes with the same shape. Reflected or rotated copies count as congruent, not new non-congruent triangles.

activities.title: Correspondence notation: △ABC ≅ △DEF
steps: Given a pair of triangles with matched tick-marks on equal sides and arcs on equal angles, identify which vertex matches which.
Write the congruence statement in the form △ABC ≅ △___ so that the letter order pairs matching vertices.
From your statement, read off which sides are equal and which angles are equal, without looking back at the diagram.
Check: does the position of each letter in the two names point to a genuinely matching part? Mark the corresponding parts first, then write the statement.
Given a WRONG statement whose letters pair non-matching parts, correct it and explain what went wrong.
activities.insight: The order of letters in a congruence statement encodes the correspondence: matching positions name matching vertices, sides and angles. The statement is only correct when every paired position is a genuinely equal part.

activities.title: Classify and reason: one, none or many?
steps: For each given data set, answer: which criterion applies (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS) — or none — and does it produce one triangle, none, or more than one?
When shown 'two sides and an angle', state explicitly whether the angle is between the two sides (SAS) or opposite one of them (SSA) before deciding.
When shown three equal angles, decide whether the triangles must be congruent, and justify.
Match corresponding parts in a △ABC ≅ △DEF item.
For each answer, write one sentence of reasoning that names WHY the data do or do not fix a unique triangle.
activities.insight: Deciding which criterion applies and whether a data set fixes a unique triangle requires checking the included/non-included distinction and separating congruence from similarity — not pattern-matching 'two sides and an angle = SAS'.

activities.title: Construct a right triangle from hypotenuse and one side
steps: DrawAB=3cm and a perpendicular ray fromA; the angle atA is90degrees.
Draw a circle centred atB with radius5cm. Its intersection with the chosen perpendicular ray locatesC, soBC is the5cm hypotenuse andAB is the3cm side.
Compare two constructions with the same data and explain why they are congruent, including reflected or rotated copies.
activities.insight: A right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side determine a right triangle up to congruence: this isRHS, not arbitrarySSA.

checkQuestion: I give you two sides of a triangle — 6 cm and 9 cm — and an angle of 40° that is NOT between them (it sits opposite the 6 cm side). Is there exactly one such triangle, more than one, or none? Explain your reasoning.
checkAnswer: More than one (here, two). This is SSA — two sides and a non-included angle, the ambiguous case: the 6 cm side can swing to meet the base ray in two different positions, so the measurements do NOT determine a unique triangle. Only SSS, SAS, ASA (and AAS, and RHS for right triangles) force a unique triangle; SSA in general does not. The reasoning must appeal to the angle being non-included / the side being able to swing.
